paragraphs.text: A loose leaf [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from Guangxi, made in the 1990s. The style is named for the town of Liubao in [Cangwu](guangxi:wuzhou-and-cangwu), a county under the city of Wuzhou. Like every [dark tea](dark:definition), its leaf is heaped after it is made, so that warmth, moisture and microbes can darken and soften it before it is packed away to age. It was made for a market far from home: the trade believed it eased the heat and damp of the work done by [Chinese miners in Malaya](liu-bao:nanyang-trade), and it went by boat down the river to Wuzhou and out by sea.

At thirty-one years, this tea is well past the ten years after which the trade counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged). How it was stored matters as much as how long it has been kept. The trade links the slow change of these teas to [warm, wet country](guangxi:land-and-climate) and cool storehouses, where the microbes that shape a dark tea do well.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
